title: What Our Autonomous Vehicles Are Actually Thinking
summary: May creates the autonomous driving system that lets ride-hail vehicles reason through the road in real time. Built for safer streets, smoother rides and…
body_markdown:
*By Jacob Crossman, SVP of Autonomy Engineering*


When you take a ride in an autonomous vehicle, May Mobility aims to make it as unremarkable as possible. Slow down and stop for a yellow light. Wait behind a delivery truck, then pass when clear. Nudge left to give a cyclist room. Nothing dramatic. Everything as expected.


But there is a lot that goes into that unremarkable ride behind the scenes. May Mobility has developed an autonomy architecture different from any other AV system on the market and it’s improving the way AVs think.


## The Standard Approach and Its Problem


The trendy way to build an autonomous vehicle right now is to take what the camera sees and translate those pixels into actions, such as gas, brake, and steer. Feed billions of miles of driving footage into a large neural network, and train it to output the right action for whatever it sees. The idea is that, if you can collect all the situations a car might encounter, you can train it to handle them all.


The problem is that driving is extraordinarily variable. Humans don’t spend all night, every night, thinking deep thoughts about what edge case they’re going to encounter the next day. And it’s clear that someone who has been driving for most of their life hasn’t experienced everything that could possibly happen. And they don’t need to. There will always be situations you haven't trained on, but a human can reason through an edge case. Yet, when a purely end-to-end system encounters something outside its training distribution, the vehicle’s response can be unpredictable and unexplainable. The typical response is “let’s get more data.” This “data is everything” approach leads to multi-billion parameter models, billions of miles of training data, and expensive custom hardware to run it all.


And after all of that time, money and work, those systems still only produce a single “best” driving action at a time, offering limited visibility into why a particular action was chosen.


Fortunately, there is a better way.


## A World Model That Predicts What Comes Next


The May approach starts from a different place. To understand May’s world model, think about how a large language model works: give it the phrase "the cat is chasing the ‘blank’" and it predicts what comes next. *Mouse* , 90% probability. *Ball of yarn* , 4%. And so on down the list with increasingly unlikely possibilities.


May Mobility’s system does something similar. It is handed a sequence of tokens describing what has happened in the recent past: the traffic light turned green, the car accelerated, the jaywalker began to sprint across the intersection. From this recently observed data, the May system builds a world model, which incorporates physics, rules of the road, and even the local culture of how people behave, predicts what comes next and tells the AV to slow down to avoid the jaywalker.


That predictive capability is powerful, but it is only part of the picture. A prediction of what might happen next does not tell you what to do about it. That is where reasoning comes in.


## Running 1,000 Futures Per Second


Making predictions is not enough to effectively drive an autonomous vehicle, and the world model does more than just tell the vehicle “slow down for the jaywalker”. Instead of producing a single action, our system proposes a set of 10 to 20 candidate behaviors. Some come from learned models of how humans have driven in similar situations. Some come from mathematics and rules: things like stopping at stop signs or giving adequate space to cyclists and pedestrians. No single source has special status. And this is where reasoning comes in.


The system takes 1,000 glimpses into 1,000 different futures and simulates what would happen in each. It runs the world model in real time while the car is driving. Each simulated outcome is checked against restraints: will the AV hit anything? Does it align with applicable traffic laws? Is the ride comfortable? The policy, or action, that produces the best and safest results across those futures earns control of the vehicle.


That’s right. *Earns* . No behavior is defaulted, and that election happens continuously while we are driving, about every 200 milliseconds. That is how it makes a decision about what macro behavior it executes and then responds instantaneously to what is going on around the AV.


Here is an example. Imagine a May Mobility autonomous vehicle is driving down a street and encounters a delivery truck stopped in its lane. There is also a cyclist, a pedestrian on the sidewalk, and an incoming car coming down the road in the adjacent lane.


An end-to-end black box system might think, “the typical behavior for that incoming car ** is to go to the edge of its lane and pass the cyclist, making space for us to pass the truck.” And it will probably be right. But our system goes further. Even if the most likely outcome is that the adjacent car stays in its lane, May Mobility’s system simulates the rarer safety cases too. Maybe its deep-learned policy does say you should pass that truck right now; that is what humans normally do. But then it double-checks itself and wonders, “What if that car swings wide? The probability is low, but the cost of a conflict is high.” So the system decides to wait a beat, let the adjacent car clear, and then pass the truck.


That is deliberative reasoning, not just predicting the most likely future, but evaluating the full range of futures and choosing the behavior that steers outcomes toward the ones you want. And that is what is happening over and over again in a drive. It is very frequent.


## The Best of Both Worlds


It is interesting to see how this actually plays out in a real drive. It is not that the deep learning models take over in complex situations and the rule-based models handle simple ones. It is that they are always interleaving, decision by decision.


Think of it this way: any gaps in the learned model — situations where the ML has not quite seen this scenario before — get covered by the mathematical, rule-based policies for fractions of a second. And simultaneously, any gaps in the rules — places where rigid mathematics would produce a clunky or overly cautious response — get covered by the learned policies. They check each other constantly.


That cooperation is what allows the system to handle situations the first time it encounters them, without needing to have seen the exact scenario in training data.


## 20,000 Miles, Not 20 Million


May Mobility’s autonomy architecture pushes the limits of what AVs could do before. May’s world model and multi-policy reasoning engine can demonstrate reliable driving within 20,000 miles, not the 20 million or even billion miles that other autonomy systems may require.


What’s more, this technology can be deployed to each of our sites with minimal adjustments based on local laws or ODD elements. The ability to deploy a general-purpose AV system that can navigate complex and novel situations — both by learning from past drives and reasoning in real time — makes May Mobility’s technology uniquely suited to scale. This is why we can use off-the-shelf compute hardware, why we can scale to new cities without rebuilding from scratch, and why our engineers can audit the system's decision-making in ways that black-box approaches do not allow.


Smarter AVs. Safer streets. Autonomy at scale. That’s what we are building, and it’s truly remarkable.

## About the Author


Jacob Crossman is senior vice president of autonomy at May Mobility, Inc. He was appointed to the position in August of 2021 and is responsible for the company’s autonomy engineering and robotics engineering functions and leads his teams in the development and deployment of May Mobility’s autonomous vehicles. Crossman joined May Mobility with more than 20 years of professional experience in research and development of autonomous sense/react technologies at Soar Technology, Inc. and Deepgram, where he served in various senior roles. He has a Master of Science and a Bachelor of Science in computer science from the University of Michigan.
